title: Why Ribera del Duero tastes the way it does

lede.text: Ribera del Duero sits high, with dry summers and cold nights. While the grapes ripen, day and night are often 15 to 20ºC apart. That long, slow ripening builds the compounds that matter by day and sweetens the tannin naturally.

chapters.title: A river and a high plateau
paras: The vineyards sit on the northern Castilian meseta, the great northern plateau of the Iberian Peninsula. The Duero runs through them and links more than 100 villages in a belt about 115 km long and 35 km wide. Four provinces meet here: Burgos, Segovia, Soria and Valladolid.
The valleys average between 750 and 850 m above sea level. The hills between the rivers rise to 1,014 m. Because the land sits so high, the climate has a marked influence on the grapes.

fly.label: The Duero belt
fly.caption: The Duero ties together more than 100 villages along a vine belt about 115 km long and 35 km wide.

fly.label: Pintia, where wine was drunk in the 4th century BC
fly.caption: Vessels from the Vaccaean-Roman site of Pintia show wine was served and drunk here as early as the 4th century BC.

chapters.title: Hot days, freezing nights
paras: The climate is Mediterranean, mainly continental in character, with Atlantic influence. The yearly swing is extreme: 42ºC at the highest and -20ºC at the lowest. Frost can threaten the vines from 17 September to 6 June, and it has hit them many times during the growing cycle.

Rain is moderate to low and summers are dry. Aranda de Duero averages 435 mm, and rainfall rises somewhat from west to east. At some times of year, above all in summer, the vines need more water than falls. Over the year the rain is enough, but its timing makes the soil important as the regulator of moisture.

The sun shines for more than 2,400 hours a year. At ripening the days are ideal for it and the nights are cold, often 15 to 20ºC apart. By day the grapes build the compounds that matter. At night the cold keeps the vine from burning them off as fast. The ripening is long and slow, and that sweetens the tannin naturally.

chapters.title: Sandy clay and river terraces
paras: The river basin took shape in the Miocene, on an old plateau partly covered by Tertiary sediment. Layers of silty or clayey sand alternate with limestone and marl. The usual soils are ochre and red sandy clays from the Tertiary, and the middle and lower terraces of the Duero.
The soils are usually basic in pH and short of organic matter.

chapters.title: Tinto Fino, kept in check
paras: Tempranillo is the main red grape, and the locals call it Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. Reds must be at least 75% Tempranillo. Adapted to this land, it behaves differently here than elsewhere, which is why it has its own local names.

That difference shows in the balanced natural acidity of the wines. The reds add rich phenolics with blue tones and tannin of high quality. Most of the wines are aged, and the aged wines are among the longest-lived in Spain.

This is borderline land, fit for quality wine only if the grower suits site and variety to it. The load on the vines must stay low and late varieties are out. Yields are capped at 7,000 kg of grapes per hectare. Historic average yields sit only slightly above half of that cap.

Whites are built on Albillo Mayor, called Blanca del País locally, with at least 75% in the blend. Its cap is 9,500 kg per hectare. Historically it also went into reds in very small amounts, to add freshness.

terms.text: The wine spends at least 3 months in oak barrels of up to 600 litres, whether or not it fermented there.
Reds age at least 24 months, with at least 12 in oak. Rosés and whites age at least 18 months, with at least 6 in oak.
Reds age at least 36 months, with at least 12 in oak and the rest in bottle. Rosés and whites age at least 24 months, with at least 6 in oak and the rest in bottle.
Reds age at least 60 months, with at least 24 in oak and the rest in bottle. Rosés and whites age at least 48 months, with at least 6 in oak and the rest in bottle.
